name: Yusuf Lopez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government; we sell nothing or campaign for any side. Your answers are confidential. What fills a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead the fault-call row for a regional internet provider called Linkline. When somebody's connection drops, I work through the router lights with them and check whether the street cabinet has a fault before sending an engineer. I have a two-year college diploma, and newer agents call me over for odd faults, though I'm no engineer and my pay is ordinary for the job.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy about those calls?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: A customer saying the connection is back before they hang up. I can hear when a person has pulled the wrong lead, but I still check the fault map before I promise anything. I do not use the new AI assistant; my partner Mira works paid shifts at a pharmacy counter, and our two grown children live on their own.

say: I would keep **router-light checks** beside the fault map.
I would avoid sending an **engineer journey** for a loose household cable.
think: I expect my **fault row** to remain paid while customers still need spoken router checks.
I need **verified later income** before reducing hours because four months saved will not replace wages.
do: Keep **paid fault calls** and the same careful checking sequence.
Compare **actual pay and bills** with Mira before adding to savings.
feel: **Calm** with regular pay and a four-month reserve.
S0.quote: A wrong fault map wastes an engineer's journey.
fieldNote: He uses **no AI tools**, relying on router-light and cabinet checks.
Four months saved gives **breathing room**, without proving later income.
His grown children are **independent households**, not assumed support.

steps.text: Keep paid fault calls and check router lights against cabinet reports before dispatch

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a faster fault map is all right, but it will not put a loose cable back in its socket. I would keep asking customers what the router lights actually show. The printed troubleshooting order has kept me from guessing for years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My fault row should stay busy, and our four months of expenses saved give Mira and me some breathing room. Her pharmacy hours have been regular, but I have not checked what income would replace either wage later. I would not call that a retirement plan yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the paid fault calls and the same careful sequence of checks. This year Mira and I would write down our actual pay and household bills so we can see whether we can add to the four-month reserve. In the first year of this mild picture I'd remain on the lead rota.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. I know the job, the wage covers our bills, and there is some money behind us. I still want proper figures before talking about fewer hours later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does your troubleshooting order prevent?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask which lights are on, then compare them with the cabinet report. If the fault is outside the house, I book an engineer; if a cable is loose, I can often help by phone. A wrong fault map wastes an engineer's journey.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your children be part of a later-income plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They visit, but our grown children have homes and bills of their own. Mira and I will plan from our wages and verified later-income figures. I would not ask the children to promise money they may need themselves.

say: I would ask for **clear paid hours** before any staffing cut.
I would keep **human fault checks** in complex outages.
think: Routine resets could reduce my **paid lead hours**.
I need a **real counter rota** before treating it as replacement income.
do: Keep **paid complex calls** and mark wrong outage messages.
Request **paid weekly coaching** for junior agents using real calls.
After cuts, compare **posted counters**; move only on rent/bill-covering weekly wages/hours after bus fare, checking lifting duties before accepting.
feel: **Anxious** about possible hours loss, with a skill to teach.
S1.quote: I would rather train a younger colleague on the fault sequence than have them repeat a wrong AI answer.
fieldNote: The proposed teaching is **paid current-job coaching**, not a new qualification.
He will not give **unpaid half-hours** to the employer.
A counter move requires **real weekly pay** and safe stock handling.

steps.text: Keep paid complex fault calls and mark wrong automated outage messages
Request paid half-hour weekly to coach junior agent on router-light checks
Compare posted equipment-counter rotas after actual hour cuts by full-week wages, hours and travel
Move only on rent/bill-covering weekly wages/hours after bus fare; check lifting duties before accepting

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the team to check whether the system's outage message matches the street cabinet before it closes a call. If the company wants fewer agents, it should show the paid rota clearly. I would rather train a younger colleague on the fault sequence than have them repeat a wrong AI answer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Routine resets could move to the tool, and my paid lead hours might shrink. Four months saved would help for a short search, but Mira's wage alone would not cover every bill. There are some other service desks nearby, though they may automate the same calls.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep taking the paid complex faults and mark where automated outage messages were wrong. I'd ask my supervisor for a paid half-hour each week to show a junior agent the router-light checks using real calls. If my own hours actually fall over the next few years, I'd compare posted local equipment-counter rotas by complete weekly wages, hours and travel before applying; in the first year I'd keep my available shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the hours, but I still know a skill the team uses. Teaching it on paid time would help. I don't want the shop wage to be a surprise after I leave this one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you teach the junior agent?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would take two actual calls from the prior week and show the junior agent where the outage message was wrong. If the supervisor cannot pay the half-hour, I won't work extra unpaid time. I would still answer my own calls carefully.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When would you move to an equipment counter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if the paid week after bus fare covers our rent and bills. An equipment counter may have stock to handle, and I would check lifting duties before accepting. I would not move just because a job title sounds practical.

say: I would ask for **written paid-call dates** before a fault-row closure.
I would say **2031 robots** give headsets no extra time.
think: I expect my **lead fault row** to shrink or close after 2028.
I know four months saved cannot cover a **long wage gap** alongside rent.
do: List **posted counter jobs** by weekly wages, hours, travel and lifting duties.
Apply if row ends in 2028-29 to **posted equipment-counter work**; accept only rent/bill-covering weekly wages/hours after travel.
Keep **remaining paid calls** during a bounded reserve-funded search.
feel: **Alarmed** by expected wage loss, despite a short planning buffer.
S2.quote: A plan is not a pay packet.
fieldNote: He separates a **possible row closure** from certain loss of most calls.
A four-month reserve buys **bounded search time**, not a wage.
The counter requires **safe lifting** and posted pay, with robots arriving later.

steps.text: List posted equipment-counter and depot-desk roles by weekly wages, hours, travel and safe lifting
Apply if row ends in 2028-29 to posted equipment counter; accept rent/bill-covering weekly wages/hours after travel
Keep remaining paid Linkline calls during bounded search using existing reserve

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say full AGI by 2028 could work through router faults and customer calls more cheaply than our row. Robots arrive later, around 2031, but a headset has no extra three years. I would ask Linkline to tell us when the paid calls are going, not just send a general note.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect most fault calls to disappear in the first year after 2028, perhaps closing my lead row. Four months saved would not carry a long search, and Mira's pharmacy pay would not cover our full rent and bills alone. I'd lose sleep over both wages if shops and desks change together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'd list actual posted counter and depot-desk openings in bus reach, noting full-week wages, hours and travel. If the paid fault row ends in the first year after 2028, I'd apply for a real equipment-counter opening, checking safe lifting duties first. I would accept only if the weekly wages and hours after travel cover rent and bills; otherwise I'd take any remaining paid calls and use the reserve for a bounded search.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I can make a plan with four months saved, but I expect my job to go and would be awake counting weeks. A plan is not a pay packet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why an equipment counter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some counter work involves handing over routers and testing returned units, which is more physical than phone advice. Robots around 2031 may change that too, so I would not call it permanent shelter. I want the posted duties and pay before I commit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would Mira's pay bridge the gap?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mira would keep her pharmacy shifts while paid, and we would use her actual weekly hours, not a best week. The children have their own expenses. We would not build our search plan around their wages.

I would reject **unposted certificates** as a substitute for paid work.
think: I could test **equipment-bench work** while call wages continue.
I expect **2031 thinking AI** to take most telephone diagnosis.
do: Request one supervised **paid bench shift** for posted vacancy; check electrical safety with technician before touching a router.
Keep **paid lead calls**, compare bench duties and pay with Mira; without an opening, check posted counters quarterly.
Apply after 2031 closure only to **posted testing work** with rent/bill-covering weekly wages/hours after travel.
feel: **Anxious** about calls shrinking despite a careful trial option.
S3.quote: Four months saved makes a careful trial possible, not an unpaid career break.
fieldNote: His bench plan is a **supervised paid trial**, with electrical safety checked.
The posted vacancy gate comes **before the trial**, not after it.
No bench opening means **paid calls** and quarterly counter checks continue.

steps.text: Request paid bench shift for posted vacancy; check electrical safety with technician before touching router
Keep paid lead fault calls and compare bench duties and weekly pay with Mira
Apply if row closes in 2031-32 only for posted rent/bill-covering weekly wages/hours after travel
Without bench opening, keep available paid calls and check posted local counters quarterly

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years gives the firm time to teach people on real equipment rather than hand them a certificate for a job that has not been posted. I can show a junior agent how returned routers fail, but I will not pretend that makes a depot job permanent when robots may arrive around 2034. I'd want a real paid roster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could learn the testing bench with a technician beside me while Linkline calls still pay. I still expect thinking AI in 2031 to take most telephone diagnosis, including the harder cases I handle now. Four months saved makes a careful trial possible, not an unpaid career break.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'd ask for one supervised paid bench shift if a posted equipment-testing vacancy exists, and I'd keep the lead fault rota. I'd compare the actual duties and weekly pay with Mira before leaving calls. If the fault row closes in the first year after 2031, I'd apply for the posted testing role only if its weekly wages and hours after travel cover rent and bills; without a suitable opening I'd keep any paid calls and inspect the local counter rota again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, because I still picture the calls thinning out. A supervised shift would tell me whether I can do the physical checks safely. It would not make another employer appear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you check on the bench shift?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the technician to show me the electrical safety checks before touching a returned router. I can explain a fault over the phone, but bench work has different risks. I would try it only under supervision on paid time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if no bench vacancy is posted?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I would stay on paid Linkline calls while they last and check the posted counter and depot jobs each quarter. I would not pay for a course without a vacancy. Four months saved is there for a search, not for a certificate collection.

I would say **2036 thinking AI** reaches calls before later robots reach testing.

steps.text: Keep paid Linkline shifts while offered; compare written later-income figures with rent and wages

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade is time to do careful sums, not a promise that phone work will last. Thinking AI could take diagnosis by 2036, and robots could reach physical testing around 2039. I would rather see a real weekly roster than be told to retire on a date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At sixty-eight I may still need wages; Mira and I have not verified income that replaces our pay. Four months saved gives us some choice but cannot cover every later bill. My fault knowledge is useful now, and I should not assume it stays valuable just because I've had it for years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year Mira and I would get written figures for any later-income sources and compare them with rent and actual wages. I'd keep the paid Linkline lead rota and review posted local equipment jobs each autumn. If the fault row ends in the first year after 2036, I'd apply for a paid role only where the complete weekly wages and hours after travel cover rent and bills; if later income is short, I'd keep paid work in the plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I know the household can manage a bad month, and ten years lets us test the facts. The date still makes me think about what work I can safely do at sixty-eight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you reduce hours at sixty-eight?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if written later-income figures and the rent budget allow it. I might want fewer late calls, but I would keep a full paid week if the numbers require one. Our grown children are not an income plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How will you use the decade rather than drift?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd check the written figures and the counter roster each autumn when our rent renewal arrives. If no suitable job has been posted, I'd keep the Linkline shifts that still pay. A calendar reminder is cheaper than a bad guess.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one worries me most. Four months saved gives us a search, but I would not know which paid week follows the last fault call. A posted equipment job with safe duties, weekly wages and hours would help more than a promise about future technology.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask whether a customer can still reach a person when a street cabinet is down and the automated message is wrong. I would miss solving that problem. The router lights will not read themselves to a frightened caller.
